title: Eight Black Candidates Vie for Governor in Historic Election Year
summary: In the 250-year history of the United States, only three Black Americans have ever been elected governor. This November, that number could more than double. Eight Black major-party candidates are running for governor across the country—the most ever in a single election year. They include Democrats and Republicans, men and women, from Florida to Wisconsin. The candidates themselves often downplay the historic nature of their campaigns. Florida Republican Byron Donalds, who won his primary on Tuesday, didn't mention his race in his victory speech. "Florida is a great meritocracy in America," he told reporters. "I'll let you guys write about that." Minnesota Republican Lisa Demuth, the first Black House speaker in her state, said she has "never led with any type of identity politics." But she added, "I recognize the historic state we are in right now." Others are more direct about why representation matters. Nevada Democrat Aaron Ford, the state's first Black attorney general, said some issues in the African American community "get ignored and don't have a voice." He pointed to voting rights, civil rights, and economic opportunity. Maryland Governor Wes Moore, the only Black governor currently in office, said his historic status is "not an applause line" but a challenge. He criticized his own party for not doing enough to support Black candidates, especially in the South. "Governors, in many ways, are becoming the last lines of defense against what we're seeing in Washington," Moore said, referencing the Supreme Court's recent redistricting decision and President Trump's attacks on diversity initiatives. Karen Finney, a Democratic strategist, said Black politicians are often the first to raise issues like maternal mortality and sickle cell disease—problems that hit Black communities harder. "These are people who have the power to shape our lives, and they shape the agenda," she said. The path to the governor's mansion has been notoriously difficult for Black politicians. Douglas Wilder of Virginia became the first elected Black governor in 1990. Since then, only Deval Patrick of Massachusetts and Moore have followed. Stacey Abrams, who narrowly lost two races in Georgia, recalled white Democratic donors funding her primary opponent in 2018. This year, the slate includes Keisha Lance Bottoms in Georgia, Jermaine Johnson in South Carolina, David Crowley in Wisconsin, and John James in Michigan. Former New York Governor David Paterson, who was not elected but ascended to the office in 2008, celebrated the bipartisan nature of the field. "This is one day when maybe the Democrats and Republicans could stand in front of a statue of George Washington and let him know that we're finally getting it right," he said. Whether any of these candidates wins remains to be seen. But one thing is certain: the 2026 midterms will be a historic test of whether America is ready to elect more Black governors.
why_it_matters: These elections will show whether state-level leadership is becoming more representative of the country and could shift state policies on health, civil rights, and voting in ways that affect young people's futures.

background_read: Black Americans have held top federal offices, but governorships have remained a stubborn barrier. Douglas Wilder (a former Virginia governor and the first Black American elected to that office in 1990) broke the color line, and Deval Patrick (a former Massachusetts governor) later joined him. Wes Moore (Maryland's current governor and the only Black governor now in office) has described his role as a challenge rather than an applause line. Stacey Abrams (a Georgia Democrat who narrowly lost two races for governor) has spoken publicly about the difficulty of raising money against white opponents. Historically, party donors and support networks have often been slower to invest in Black statewide candidates, especially in the South. Governors control state budgets, schools, and voting procedures, so these races affect policy far beyond Washington. The 2026 midterms will test whether a record field of eight Black candidates can overcome those longstanding obstacles.

perspectives.description: For supporters, the record field is a sign that both parties are opening doors to Black candidates. Winning more governorships would give Black leaders direct control over state budgets, schools, and voting rules.

Critics point out that only three Black candidates have ever won a governor's race. Stacey Abrams remembered donors funding her opponent, and Wes Moore accused his own party of failing to invest in Black candidates, especially in the South.
The candidates' reluctance to run on race shows that identity politics is not a simple strategy. In some states, stressing records and local issues may matter more than making history.
The 2026 midterms will reveal whether the increase in candidates translates into actual wins. If several win, future campaigns may see more money and party support for Black statewide candidates.
